title: Australian researchers find Bluetooth trailer brakes could be applied by anyone nearby
excerpt: Researchers in Tasmania found that some Bluetooth trailer brake controllers accepted brake commands without pairing. The maker has released fixes for two models; one older model is still waiting.

sources.title: iTnews: Hackers can slam on Bluetooth-connected trailer brakes, researchers find
Cybernews: Bluetooth trailer brake vulnerability lets attackers trigger brakes
The420.in: Bluetooth Flaws Let Hackers Control Trailer Brakes Without Authentication, CISA Warns
Hackaday: This Week In Security: Federal Breaches, Leaky AI Routers, PhpAfterShell, Bluetooth Trailer Brakes
US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency: ICS Advisory ICSA-26-323-02

body_html:
Two security researchers in Australia have found that some Bluetooth-controlled trailer brake controllers would accept a brake command from any phone or device within Bluetooth range, without pairing, a PIN or a password. The maker, Elecbrakes, an Australian company that sells mainly in Australia and New Zealand, has released fixed firmware for two of the three affected models. No real-world misuse has been reported.

A trailer brake controller tells the brakes on a caravan, horse float or other trailer when to slow down along with the towing vehicle. Elecbrakes controllers are set and adjusted from a phone app or an in-car remote over Bluetooth.

What was found

Patrick Forck and Jeremy McCarthy of Element Digital, an IT consultancy in Tasmania, tested the EB2 and VM1 models and the older ELBC 2000. iTnews reports that the researchers found an unauthenticated device within roughly 10 to 100 metres "could apply the trailer's stoppers at full force, without pairing or authentication." Commands could also be recorded and replayed, and the firmware update channel relied on weak checks.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), which publishes advisories on industrial and connected equipment, issued advisory ICSA-26-323-02 on 19 November 2026, according to Cybernews and The420.in. Three vulnerabilities are listed: CVE-2026-96805 and CVE-2026-125273, each rated 9.6 out of 10, and CVE-2026-124281, rated 6.1. As reported, CISA says an attacker could take control of the brakes, change firmware, disable brake lights or change other safety settings. The brakes release when the connection drops, but an attacker who stays in range could keep them applied.

The response

According to iTnews, the researchers told Elecbrakes on 18 May 2026, and the company released fixes on 6 July: EB2 firmware 3.0.4.4.3 and VM1 firmware 1.3.4.2.1. Brake control now requires authenticated pairing, Hackaday reports. Owners must start the update themselves in the app. Elecbrakes told iTnews that 60 to 70 percent of controllers connecting each day are on the latest firmware, and that it has notified 39,843 users. It said it has had no reports of injury or damage.

The disclosure took about six months, including a 53-day gap with no reply from the company, iTnews reports. The firmware images are still not digitally signed; Elecbrakes says it addressed the risk "at a different layer of the stack". The older ELBC 2000 has no fix yet, and a separate fix is being worked on.

What owners can do

  • Open the Elecbrakes app, check your model and firmware version, and install the update if offered.
  • For the ELBC 2000, which has no fix yet, the reports advise keeping the controller actively connected to your own phone or remote, as the product instructions say.

What is still unknown

It is not known how many controllers are still running old firmware, when the ELBC 2000 fix will arrive, or when firmware signing will be added. We could not open CISA's advisory or the researchers' write-up directly; the details above come from the reports listed.

Which Directives cover this risk

A brake is a safety function, so this touches Directive 3: Physical safety and Directive 6: Secure and supported: a product that can move or stop a vehicle should only take commands from its owner, and fixes should reach people quickly. Directive 1: Always stoppable is about people keeping control, which includes control over who else can send commands. Directive 9: Accountable covers how makers answer security reports. As our security page puts it, a hacked robot is one nobody is in charge of, and the same holds for any connected device.

Questions you can ask any maker

  • Does the device need pairing or a PIN before it accepts commands?
  • How will I know about a security update, and is it installed automatically?
  • Are firmware updates digitally signed?
  • How do you handle reports from security researchers, and how fast do you respond?

More questions are on our questions to ask page. Findings like this, reported and fixed, are why independent security standards for connected products exist, not a reason to fear the technology.
